en: Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Guru. Having first recollected the glorious Guru and offered arghya to the Sun;
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs, and having prepared the vessel for the general offering (sāmānyārghapātra).
Having gone to the eastern gate and having performed purification through inspection and so forth, one should worship.
Having worshipped Śānti at the archway (toraṇa), one should worship the jar (ghaṭa) belonging to the Śāntikalā-tattva.
Then there is Bhūloka, then Bhuvarloka, and then Pradyumna, the illuminator.
One should worship Śoma and Aṅgāra on one's own left and right; one should conquer the pitcher [of the deity], and likewise Nandin to its right, and Mahākāla within the pitcher.
One should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā to its right, as well as the Ṛgveda and the Kṛtayuga;
and one should worship the river Praśānta and Śiśira at Kalasa.
In this clockwise sequence, these should be worshipped with their seed-syllables and their own names;
one should worship Gaṇa, Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī at the Uduṃbara tree.
One should worship Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ with the trident in due order;
likewise, one should worship Īśvarādhipati, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghoravargaka at the threshold.
At the gate, this [deity] should be worshipped in sequence; one should place Kumuda at the flagstaff.
One should worship those adorned with banners with the mantra ending in *vajra hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having offered the bali-oblation to Hetuka, these [deities] are considered to reside in the ears and other sense organs.
Then, in the corners starting from the southeast, one should worship Siddhika on the plantain tree,
Kumudākṣa on the banner, and Śaktika on the flag.
Having performed worship, one should offer a bali-oblation to the Destroyer of Tripura using his own mantra.
Then, at the southern gate, having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, one should worship the Bhūti-archway;
in the pitcher, one should worship the Vidyā-kalās:
Svarloka, Maharloka, Ajaghna, and Jaghna.
Budha and Bṛhaspati are to be worshipped on the two branches to one's left;
to their east, in the jar, Bhṛṅgirīṭi Vināyaka is to be worshipped.
In the pitcher to his east, at the junction, Yama should be worshipped;
between him and the Yamaghaṭa, Mahimā and Narmadā are to be worshipped again in the pitcher to the west.
One should worship the Yajurveda as the Tretā Yuga in that western jar;
one should worship those named Parjanya and Aśoka in the river-pitcher.
One should worship Gaṇa, Śaravatī, and Lakṣmī at the Ūrdhvodumbaraka;
and Bhaga, Indra, Parjanya, Rudra, and Ādhipati at the Śūla.
One should worship Aghora and the *ṭa*-group on the banner, and the *puṇḍarīka* on the flag;
and on the staff, one should worship with the mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the fire Vetāla, one should worship him.
Then, in the south-western corners, one should sprinkle with that water.
One should worship Kīrttikā on the plantain tree and Vāmanākṣa on the banner;
having worshipped Khaḍgaka on the flag, one should offer an oblation to Yamajihvā and ask for forgiveness.

Then, having gone to the western gate, one should sprinkle it with the *prokṣa-śara* mantra; having worshipped the archway (*toraṇa*) at the entrance, one should worship the *nivṛtti-kalā* in the water-pot.
Then, to his left, one should worship Aja, Tvaṣṭṛ, Loka, Tapas, as well as Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ;
one should worship these at the two door-posts.
One should worship Venus, Saturn, and Rāhu, and then worship the pitcher (ghaṭa) to their north;
Taurus (Vṛṣa) should be worshipped on the pitcher, as well as the Indus and the Śarāvatī rivers.
One should worship the Yuga and the Dvāpara, as well as the two Śāma-vedas and the jar;
one should worship the Bhūtasaṃjīvanākṣa and the Amṛtoghaghaṭa.
One should worship Gaṇa, Śaravatī, and Lakṣmī at the Urdhvodumbaraka;
one should worship Aryaman, Mitra, and Tvaṣṭṛ upon the tridents.
One should worship Nārāyaṇādhipati and Sadyojāta;
likewise, one should worship the group of mantras beginning with Tapa and the Astra-mantra at the threshold.
One should offer an oblation to Kālākṣa upon the banner, a spike upon the ear, and a noose upon the flag, along with offerings such as incense, lamps, and other pleasing gifts.
Then, in the corners starting from the northwest (Vāyavya), one should worship Dhṛti on the plantain tree;
likewise, one should worship Sarvanetra on the flagstaff and Dhvaja on the banner.
One should offer incense, lamps, and other pleasing offerings to Karālin.
Then, at the northern gate, the knower of mantras should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra;
having worshipped health (Ārogya) upon the archway (toraṇa), he should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) upon the jar of the Kalās.
Satyaloka and Dhruvaloka, as well as Āvaha and Vivaha,
are the guardians of the gateway of the region, positioned naturally on the left and right in sequence.
Having worshipped Rāhu and Bhūghaṭa, one should worship the goddess Caṇḍī in the two jars;
Tāpikā and Payoṣṇī are to be worshipped in the jar on one's own left side.
One should worship Vedhas, Utharva, and Kali in the pitcher situated to the east of that;
and Dhanada and Śrīpada should be worshipped in the river-pitcher at some point.
One should worship Gaṇa, Śaravatī, and Lakṣmī at the Ūrdhvodumbaraka;
and Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, and Aṃśumat at the Triśūlaka.
Brahmādhipati is in the north-east, Vāmadeva likewise in the upper [direction];
Yaśasvargī is at the threshold, and Sumukha at the banner.
Having offered the bali-oblation with the mantra "gadā ye hūṃ phaṭ" at the banner and at each of the two fields,
one should first perform the propitiation of the deity with incense and other offerings.
One should worship Puṣṭika after sprinkling [the site] with the *ayaiśāne* mantra; one should worship the deity named Suprasiddha on the banner and Triśūlaka on the flag.
Having worshipped with the mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should offer the *bali* for Bhīmadarpa;
then, one should worship according to the sequence upon the upper banner (*ūrddhapatākā*).
One should worship Siddhi, Kīrti, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, and Nityā in the pillars of plantain trees at the corners from the southeast to the northeast; one should perform the worship with them.
The earth-element is said to reside in the trunks [of trees], the water-element in grass and similar things,
the fire-element in barren [plants], and the air-element is considered to be in the stalks.
The five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta are said to be the pillars and the canopy.
Then, having arrived at the western gate, they were sprinkled with that water by means of the descent of the divine vision that follows after the divine [state].
Having cast flowers into the sky with the *jvalanārāca* weapon,
he struck those stationed on the ground— of all three types— with three blows from his right feet.
The practitioner of mantra should dispel the obstacles from the center of the sacrificial pavilion.
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the power of Śiva’s speech.
Crossing the threshold slightly while leaning toward the left side,
he should enter with his right foot and place the weapon-mantra upon the threshold-post.
Having closed the remaining doors, one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstupati) in the center;
then, having proceeded by way of circumambulation, one should sit down to the right of the deity.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and so forth, one should practice the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Having expelled the breath through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī] and having drawn it back in through the *iḍā* (the left), one should proceed.
And having stabilized it with the middle [channel], one should then release that wind.
By abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, one should dissolve [the breath] gradually into the dvādaśānta;
there is a lotus consisting of Śiva, brilliant white, pouring forth abundant nectar.
One should always meditate upon [the deity] situated on the forehead, with a pericarp fashioned from the moon;
the body, flooded by that nectar, becomes newly arisen, firm, and whole.
And within that, one should contemplate the individual soul (jīva) as having the nature of consciousness, yet not [identical] with it.
First, one should contemplate the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as follows: from Śiva arises the Command (ājñā), from that the Piṇḍa, and from that again the Subtle (sūkṣma);
from that [arises] the Supreme (para), and from the Supreme those two arise mutually. Thus indeed is the contemplation of the purification of the elements.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to this sequence of the guru’s instruction.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) and so forth upon the body, one should again perform the placement and so forth upon the face.
And having thus divided [the victim] into pieces, one should perform the sacrifice in the intermediate space. As follows:

Upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, seated on a corpse-throne (pretāsana) such as Ananta and others, and established upon a lion-throne brought forth by contemplation, one should satisfy the Blessed Lord through offerings of faith, heaps of flowers, fruits, and so forth. By means of the blissful mass of the wonder of one's own consciousness, within the state of non-duality, one should contemplate the manifestation of Śiva-nature. This is the inner sacrifice (antaryāga).
Then, taking the vessel for the *argha* offering, one should wash it and fill it with water while meditating on the black nectar (*kṛṣṇa-pīyūṣa*) upon the forehead.
Water, milk, kuśa grass, tantrāla, manasā, sesame seeds,
along with barley and white mustard— these are declared to be the eight components of the bath for the removal of sin.

Having fulfilled these requisites, one should worship with the six-limbed root mantra; having offered sandalwood and unbroken rice grains, one should gratify [the deity] with the *dhenumudrā*; having protected it with the *astra-mantra* and veiled it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should likewise protect oneself with that.

Sprinkle [the area]. Sprinkle the sacrificial materials with the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Having worshipped the seat of the self and the form of the self, and having applied the forehead mark (*tilaka*), one should begin the purification of the mantra.

Having raised the fire from the place of Kaṇḍakṣa and Ulūnī through the sequence of the wheel of seasons (ṛtucakra) into the center, one should take refuge in the manifestation of consciousness (cidvyakti) therein.
Having meditated upon Ānandamara at midday, while recollecting the mantra here.
Then this purification of the mantra and the practitioner's wheel occurs.
Having purified [the area] with this, one should prepare a circular mandala of sandalwood paste on one's own right hand;
having accomplished the protection with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains, one should worship the deity.
Having visualized it in the form of a shimmering star, one should place it upon one's own head.

Then, thinking "I am the omniscient one; my sacrifice is the most important," and having again uttered the root mantra with pride, he should wrap his head with his own white turban. Thereafter, he should adorn his own body with perfumes, garments, and ornaments.
With bracelets and other ornaments, with necklaces, armlets, and anklets and other decorations.
Then, having consecrated the *vikirāṇa* with the Aghora-weapon mantra, and having consecrated the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) with the Pāśupata-weapon mantra.

Having fashioned [the blade] from *darbha* grass to the measure of a palm tree with thirty-six petals, one should empower it with the *Śivāstra* mantra recited seven times; this is the most excellent sword of awakening for the braid.
Having thus grasped the sword of knowledge, one should proceed with the five products of the cow.
In the center, one should place five compartments extending from east to north,
[inscribed with] Śiva, Sadāśiva, Vidyā, Kāla, and Puruṣa in sequence.
One should plant five vessels here: Supratiṣṭha, Suśānta, Tejas, Mṛtātmaka, and Ratnodaya. Likewise, one should plant the vessels.
Cow dung, cow urine, ghee, curd, and milk as the fifth—
these one should cast in sequence toward the west, north, south, east, and the center.
One should consecrate the cow dung and other materials with the mantras *sadyojāta*, *vāma*, *rupin*, *puruṣa*, and *īśa*, respectively, according to their sequence.
One should cast each preceding element into the fire while reciting the root mantra;
then, one should recite the root mantra eighteen times over water with *kuśa* grass while chanting the *gāyatrī*.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are declared to be the destroyer of great sins:
half an aṅguṣṭha of cow dung and one pala of cow urine.
Two palas of ghee are prescribed, and the measure of curd is three palas.
Five palas of the five-milk product [pañcagavya] and one pala-measure of kuśāmba.
One should collect the dung and urine of a black cow, the ghee of a tawny one,
the curd of a Surabhi (white) cow, and the milk of a copper-colored cow.
In the absence of all other castes, which woman is praised? A Kapilā.
An auspicious vessel made of gold, silver, palāśa wood, or copper.
This is known as the Śivakūrca, performed according to the rite of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having obtained it by reciting the root mantra eight hundred times, one should drink it all mixed together in one place.
Like the destruction of cotton, like fire to a forest of *sāma* grass.
The Śivakūrca destroys even the most grievous sins.
Sprinkle the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the guest-offering (arghyāmbu).
Having proceeded by way of circumambulation and stood in the south-western corner.
One should begin the consecration of the pavilion.
Perform the inspection, sprinkling, striking, sprinkling from all sides, digging, uprooting,
filling, leveling, pouring water, pounding, sweeping, smearing, the arrangement of the artistic elements, the laying of the triple-thread,
sprinkling, worship, the drawing of lines, the consecration with the *vajra*, and having gathered the materials at the four corners, construct the pavilion consisting of the artistic elements.
One should meditate.
Then, reciting the Aghora mantra, he should scatter the offerings.
Having gathered [the materials] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), a bundle of kuśa grass (kuśakūrccika), and a new broom, one should prepare the seat for the vardhanī in the northeast corner.
One should worship Śāṅga Vāstunātha between the south-west and Varuṇa (the west).

And in the west, Mahālakṣmī is to be worshipped. Having diligently meditated upon the Mukhamaṇḍapa, one should then [establish] the mobile seat with the syllable Om (praṇava), using vessels filled with water containing gems and medicinal herbs, smeared with sandalwood paste, and adorned with sprouts and flowers.
Situated in the northeast direction, one should worship him with eight flowers.
On the southern side of the pitcher, facing west and possessing the proper characteristics,
the preceptor, who is an expert in mantras, should worship with the Astra mantra.
Having worshipped the Śivāstra and the Vardhinī with their respective mantras and the six-limbed mantra.
One should worship the guardians of the directions.
Salutation to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the sovereign lord of the gods.
One should visualize Śakra, golden-hued, wearing a crown, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, possessing a thousand eyes, and holding a thunderbolt in his hand.
One should cause the offering (bali) to be presented to that [deity] by means of the root-form of the seat.
Salutation to Agni, who holds a spear in his hand and is the lord of splendor.
He possesses seven flames, wears five garlands, and holds a water-pot.
One should present an offering to him— a goat standing upon a goat, garlanded with flames and red with blood, holding a spear in its hand— which destroys all obstacles.

Salutation to Yama, who holds a staff in his hand, the lord of the ancestors. One should meditate upon Kāla, the lord of the southern direction, who is mounted upon a buffalo, holds a staff in his hand, is terrifying, and bears the noose of Time.
Salutation to the Lord of the Rakṣasas in the southwest, who holds a noose in his hand.
With blood-red eyes, mounted upon a corpse, and possessing the luster of the petals of a blue lotus.
"O Kṛpa and Aśvatthāman, drink this water that is worthy of being honored," said the lord of the Rākṣasas.
Salutation to Varuṇa, who holds a noose in his hand, the lord of the waters;
he is joyful, bearing a serpent-noose, and his body is radiant with the splendor of gems.
One should meditate upon Varuṇa, white as the moon, seated upon a makara.
Salutation to Vāyu, who holds a banner in his hand, the lord of the vital breaths;
he possesses a yellowish-green luster and bears a swaying banner.
And [he saw] Samīraṇa, the vital breath of all beings, seated upon a deer.
Salutations to Kubera, who holds a mace in his hand, the lord of wealth;
Kubera, seated upon a ram, proud and of dwarfish form.
One should meditate upon the lord of the north, who has the luster of gold and holds a mace in his hand.
Salutation to Īśāna, who holds a trident in his hand, the lord of spirits;
[I salute] Īśāna, mounted upon a bull, bearing a trident and a serpent.
White as the autumn moon, with the moon as his crest and three eyes.
Salutation to Ananta, the lord of serpents, who holds a discus in his hand;
to the lotus-eyed Ananta, who is endowed with ten hoods encircling him.
One should worship him who resembles a garland of lightning and is mounted upon a tortoise.
Salutation to the Brahmin who holds a lotus in his hand, the sovereign of heaven;
[I salute] the four-faced Brahmā, who is stout, yellow-complexioned, and possesses four arms.
And he was mounted upon a swan-vehicle, carrying a staff, a rosary, and a white water-pot.
Having worshipped Kṣetrapāla in the southern jar located in the northwest corner.
Then, taking up the Astra-vardhinī vessel, which follows the auspicious pitcher with an unbroken stream of water,
he proclaimed the command of Śiva to the world-protectors while reciting the root mantra.
One should cause it to revolve in a clockwise direction.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice and for the destruction of obstacles,
you all must arm yourselves with your respective vehicles and weapons by the command of Śiva.
Reciting thus, one should first install the Śiva-kalaśa.

Thereafter, one should establish the *vardhanī* vessel. Having worshipped the Supreme Lord in the *śiva-kuṇḍa* according to the daily rite (*nityavat*), one should worship the entire collection of weapons (*astrajāta*) along with their attendants (*sāṅga*) in the *vardhanī*.
Having performed the invocation and other rites, and having offered sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and garlands;
Having recited the root mantra, one should touch the Śiva-kumbha with the thumb and the vardhanī with the fist.
The heart of Bhaga is the Liṅga, and the heart of the Liṅga is Bhaga;
salutation to that Bhagaliga, who is Umā-Rudra.
Having thus performed the consecration as the Bhaga and Liṅga, one should offer the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga).
Oṃ! You alone are the Lord of this sacrifice; this form of yours is immovable.
This is your thirtyfold [weapon]; therefore, take up your own weapon.
Having offered the sword of gnosis with the weapon-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*,
one should offer it after reciting the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times.
And the vardhanī should be made with a tenth part of the dimensions of the limbs.
Oṃ, salutations to Umā, who possesses the form of the yoni, and to Śaṅkara, who bears the form of the liṅga and bestows grace upon all.
Oṃ! Just as this sacrificial hall has been constructed with effort, O Blessed One, Lord of the World, you who are the best of all sacrificers must protect it.
Having thus made this request for protection.
Having worshipped Gaṇapati in the north-west corner, and having worshipped the Guru-kalaśa in the north-east.
Then, having worshipped the Blessed One together with his limbs (attendants) either on a sacrificial mound or within the heart of Śiva;
Having paid homage and requested permission, [he says] "I shall perform the fire-rite."
Then one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Taking the general argha vessel, one should proceed to the place of fire-offering (homasthāna) by way of circumambulation, reciting:
*oṃ hauṃ śivāya namaḥ*. [This is] the rite of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).
Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ: [this is for] sprinkling and striking.
Oṃ heṃ kavacā vaṣaṭ; [this is] the sprinkling.
Oṃ haḥ tāstrāya hūṃ phaṭ: for digging and excavating. Oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ: for filling and leveling.
Oṃ haṃ, voṣaṭ to the armor; [this is] the sprinkling.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ: the clearing away [of obstacles]. Oṃ haṃ kavacāya voṭ: the sweeping and smearing [of the site].
Oṃ hauṃ śāntyatītāye namaḥ: in the center.
Oṃ haiṃ, homage to Śānti. In the east.
Oṃ hyaṃ, homage to Vidyā. [In the] south.
Oṃ hvīṃ, homage to Pratiṣṭhā; in the north. Oṃ hlāṃ, homage to Nivṛtti; in the west.
Thus ends the conceptualization of the *kalās*.
Oṃ haṃ, homage to the armor. [Perform] the wrapping with three threads.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the sacrificial pit consisting of the digits (kalās).
Oṃ haḥ, homage to the weapon-mantra.
With the tip of a *kuśa* blade, one draws three lines extending northward and four lines extending eastward.
Reciting "Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ," one empowers [the site] by forming the shape of a *vajra* with three *kuśa* blades.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the heart! And the offering of the path is performed with two *kuśa* blades whose tips point toward the east and north.
The eighteen purificatory rites [are performed] with the root-heart mantra ending in the syllable *oṃ*.
Oṃ haṃ, homage to the armor. With kuśa grasses from the directions of the pit and the neck, one should fence off the area with two blades pointing eastward and two pointing toward the north.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī, the seat of Vāgīśvara.
He places a seat in the middle of the sacrificial pit.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara.

Therefore, from the invocation (āvāhana) up to the offering of flowers, one should perform the ritual while contemplating the two [deities], who resemble flowers and are adorned with all ornaments, engaged in mutual play.
Then, having brought the fire, [he should perform the rite] with pure bowls and other vessels.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya hūṃ phaṭ! Having drawn out the unbroken limbs, having discarded the flesh-eaters, and having purified [them] by means of the gazing and other rites.
Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the embodiment of Fire.

Having drawn out that which has the luster of the rising sun by means of the *kuśa* mudrā and the inhalation (*pūraka*) of the elemental fire, and having united with the *bindu* that which has the luster of ten thousand suns— arising from the navel-fire during the retention (*kumbhaka*)— one should merge it into oneness with that *bindu*.

Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the fire-consciousness. By means of the *recaka* breath and the *udbhava-mudrā*, expel from the right nostril that which resembles the sun, and having drawn it out, place it in the fire-vessel. Consecrate it with the six-syllable mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*), veil it with the *kavaca-mantra*, protect it with the *astra-mantra*, and [seal it] with the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having rendered the spear [of the weapon] nectar-like, one should worship it with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni. Thus it is to be worshipped.

Standing on the ground, having taken up the fire-vessel and whirled it three times clockwise around the *yoni*, one should contemplate the union of the two young ones— the Lord of Speech (*Vāgīśa*) and Umā— whose heads are in the northeast, who are mounted upon a bull,
and whose meeting occurs at the junction of the skin and the elements.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seed-syllable of Śiva. One should visualize Vāgīśī being impregnated by her husband Vāgīśa within the womb via the embryonic channel, as if she were about to conceive a seed, and cast [the seed] facing oneself.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the heart.
Thus ends the ritual for making [the deity] manifest and the covering with garments.
Oṃ hāṃ, svadhā to Vāgīśvarī.
Thus concludes the ritual of purification and sipping water.
Oṃ haṃ, homage to the armor; thus is the covering with leaves.
Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the weapon; thus is the kindling. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the fire of the womb; thus is the worship.
Oṃ haḥ, salutation to the weapon-mantra (astra). Vāgīśī holds in her hands seven weapons and bestows the kuśa grass over which the mantra has been recited.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to Sadyojāta. [This is] the fire worship.
*Oṃ hā hṛdayāya svāhā*—with five oblations of sesame seeds, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) is performed.
*Oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*—the worship is performed. *Oṃ hīṃ śirase svāhā*—with five oblations of sesame seeds.
Oṃ haṃ puṃ, obeisance to the body consisting of the eightfold city.
"One should offer a drop of water that has become a seed with the *kuśa* grass"—this is the sprinkling (*praśravaṇa*).
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. [This is] the worship.
Oṃ hraiṃ, svāhā to the Śikhā. Five oblations of sesame seeds.
With the fifteen-syllable mantra "Oṃ hyaṃ, svāhā to the Śikhā," the visualization of the faces and limbs is performed.
The opening of the mouth, the rite of atonement, and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; [this is] the worship.
Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the armor (kavaca). Offering five oblations of sesame seeds.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ; by this, the kindling of the fire. Offering drops of water for the purpose of bathing.

With the mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should spread *kuśa* grass inside and outside the girdle (*mekhalā*). Upon those [grass seats], one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of a seat of *darbha* grass with the Heart-mantra.
For the removal of saliva, there is an oblation (*homa*) of five pieces of *samī* wood with the Weapon-mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā; upon the eastern seat.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu; in the west. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śaṅkara; in the south.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta; [in the] north.

Having worshipped with the heart-mantra Indra and the other infinite world-protectors (lokapālas), situated in the east, south, west, north, above, and below, and facing the fire, [one says]: "O, O world-protectors,
please protect this child!"
Thus one should cause [the disciple] to hear the command.

Then, the purification of the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles is performed with the four [rites] beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*). Having gratified them with that [mantra] ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, one [proceeds] with that same armor-mantra (*vastreṇa*) using the tips, middles, and bases of *kuśa* grass.

Having touched the upper, middle, and lower parts of the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles—at these three locations—one performs the placement (*nyāsa*) of the three principles (*tatva*) as follows: "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-principle"; "Oṃ hīṃ, obeisance to the Knowledge-principle"; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Self-principle. Thus is the placement of the three principles.
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Śiva. [With the] *śruva* [ladle]. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śakti. [With the] *śruci* [ladle]. Having encircled [the vessel] with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and a triple thread.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles. Thus they are to be worshipped.

Having placed [the vessel] upon *kuśa* grass to its own right, and having purified the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) through the four purifications beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), one should hold it in the southeast corner of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*). By offering a drop of clarified butter with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā," one performs the heating (*tāpana*). Holding it in the northeast corner, by offering a drop of clarified butter with the mantra "Oṃ hīṃ viṣṇave svāhā," one performs the placing over the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*).
Holding the *kuṇḍa* by the navel, [recite]: *oṃ hūṃ rudrāya svāhā*. Thus is the dismissal (*udvāsana*) following the offering of a drop of clarified butter.

The *utplavana* (leaping up) is performed by means of the weapon-mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, using two *kuśa* blades to cause [the fire] to leap upward toward the face of the fire. The *saṃplavana* (submerging) is performed by means of the heart-mantra, causing [the fire] to submerge toward oneself. With the heart-mantra, one faces the *kuśa* blade upward.
"Having touched the ghee, one should cast it into the fire"—this is the purification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*). Likewise, there is the *nīrāñjana* with the *kavaca* [mantra].
There is the *dīpana* by casting burnt *kuśa* grass with the *astra* [mantra] ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having formed a *brahmagranthi* at the center of the heart with two *kuśa* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) within the clarified butter.
Therein, one should contemplate the white and black fortnights as well as the three channels.
Taking ghee from the vessel of ghee on the right side:
*Oṃ hāṃ, svā to Agni, the right eye.*
Hā on the right side; having taken ghee on the left side, [recite] "Oṃ hāṃ somāya svā" at the left eye.
Hā! On the left side of the clarified butter. Having taken the clarified butter from the middle and the top:
Oṃ hāṃ! To Agni and Soma, svāhā! In the third eye. Hā! On the middle and top of the clarified butter. Oṃ hāṃ! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, you; in the mouth of Agni.

O, for the three portions of ghee! Having consecrated [the ghee] with the six limbs of the mantra, veiled it with the *kavaca* (armor) mantra, protected it with the *astra* (weapon) mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*, and rendered it nectar-like with the *śakti* weapon ending in *voṣaṭ* and the appropriate mudrā;
then, having purified it with a drop of this ghee, one should sprinkle the remaining ghee as well.
One should place [the mantra] upon one's own face: *oṃ haṃ sadyojātāya svāhā* | *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya svāhā* |
Oṃ hūṃ aghorāya svāhā || Oṃ heṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā || Oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā ||

O Agni, there shall be oblations of clarified butter to anoint the faces at the western, northern, southern, eastern, and central mouths, with one offering for each: *oṃ haṃ hiṃ svāhā* to Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva; *oṃ hiṃ hūṃ svāhā* to Vāmadeva.
Svāhā to the two Aghoras! Oṃ hūṃ heṃ, svāhā to Aghora and Tatpuruṣa!
Oṃ haṃ hoṃ, svāhā to Tatpuruṣa and Īśāna. Oṃ hoṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ, svāhā to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta.
Thus, by means of a stream of clarified butter directed toward the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast, there is the unification of the faces.

Having meditated upon the faces: whichever face is desired for whatever rite among the five in front, one should place that face at the top; and in its place, the upward-facing mouth [should be placed]. For the birth-rite (*jātakarma*): *oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. Thus is the worship of the fire.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya svāhā—thus, five oblations of sesame seeds.
Having given it the name "Oṃ Hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations," [he should do so].
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara.
Thus ends the worship of the two.

Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarye svāhā | Oṃ hāṃ vāgiśvarāya svāhā. Having offered ten oblations of sesame seeds for each of these with [the word] "svāhā," one should dismiss these two with the mantra ending in "namaḥ. Then: Oṃ hauṃ śivāya svāhā vauṣaṭ.

Thereafter, having filled the *śruva* ladle with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and having placed a flower on the tip of the *śruk* ladle, one should slowly move it from the space between the left breasts to the heart.
Having led [the breath] to the end of the mouth or to the base of the sacrificial ladle (*śruga*),
you— O footless one— should utter the root mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ* through the movement of the central channel until its dissolution;
then, joined with the nectar from the end of the sixteen [fingers], offer the full stream that fulfills all desires.

Having performed the complete naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa), one should establish a separate fire from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the purpose of the cooked offering (caru) and for incense and lamps.
Then follows the preparation of the sacrificial oblation (caru): having constructed a hearth in the southeast corner of the pavilion, facing west.
Then, having taken the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru), wash it with the Weapon mantra (astra) and smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances using the Root mantra (mūla).

Having fumigated [the image] with incense, one should wrap it around the neck with the armor-mantra (*varma*) and the thread. Having fashioned the mandala with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should provide a seat of *kuśa* grass.
In that maṇḍala, one should worship the seats of Ananta and the others.
Having placed the vessel there, one should worship it with the root mantra along with its ancillaries.
Having removed the flower, one should pour milk with the Astra-mantra and then place rice, molasses, and other offerings with the Mūla-mantra.
Having performed the fourfold purification, beginning with the inspection of the crest-lock (cūlī), one should worship.
Oṃ, obeisance to Dharma. Oṃ, obeisance to Adharma. Therein, one should place the cooking vessel.
The opening and closing [of the vessel] are performed with the Astra-mantra. When it has sweated, the pouring of hot [melted butter] is done right there.
With the limb-mantra ending in *voṣaṭ*, one should then remove the vessel from the previously prepared maṇḍala.
One should perform the cooling sprinkling (śītābhighāra). Then, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs starting from the base, one should worship the sacrificial pit and the fire.
Oṃ hrūṃ, homage to Vadanyā. Thus is the worship.

With this very mantra ending in *svāhā*, one performs the oblation of sixteen fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Oṃ! O Agni, you are the Lord and the supreme purifying splendor; therefore, having established him within the lotus of your heart, I satisfy him.

Having thus prayed, one should meditate on the fire emerging from the right nostril, rubbing the nostril with the channel (nāḍī), and worship Śiva along with his limbs as being of the color of fire, free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi); then [one should perform] the offering of food (naivedya), purification (pavitra), recitation (japa), and so forth.

O Blessed One, having prepared [the offerings] with whatever substances are available, I shall indeed satisfy [the deities] and worship the tongue of the fire with the *saṅkeli* mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ ūṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*.
In the southwest.
Oṃ lrāṃ Kanakāye svāhā. [West]
Oṃ hrīṃ raktāyai svāhā || In the northwest.
Oṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to Kṛṣṇā; in the southeast.
Oṃ śrā-ūṃ suprabhāyai svāhā || [To] the East.
Oṃ śrā-ūṃ atiriktāyai svāhā || [To] the Northeast.
Oṃ hrūṃ bahurūpāyai svāhā. [In the center.]
The visualization of the tongue is like a stream of clarified butter extending from the southern to the northern extremity.
In some places, the name is not mentioned at all.
No; [the offerings] are performed with one's own fire. The *saṃpāta* oblations are to be offered.
Having consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra, protect it with the weapon-mantra and veil it with the armor-mantra.
One should place it before the Vardhanī vessel. Thus ends the procedure for the *caru* oblation.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should worship the radiant and supreme [deity] together with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the seat (*āsana*) within the lotus of the heart, having invoked [the deity] as before; having requested [forgiveness], one should satisfy Śiva. Having established the connection of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) between the sacrificial fire and Śiva by means of oneself, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) in the limbs from the base of the power (*śakti*).
Having offered the full oblation with the root mantra ending in *voṣaṭ* according to the ten-part division, one should again perform an oblation of sesame seeds.

Having offered the full oblation with the root mantra, one should offer the ten-fold portion to the gatekeepers and the world-protectors (lokeśas). Then, until the end of the full oblation, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with a hundred recitations of the weapon mantra (astra). Thereafter follows the illumination of the mantra.
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ hāṃ hauṃ to Śiva, haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ hāṃ, [obeisance] to the heart: haḥ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ hīṃ; haḥ hūṃ phaṭ to the head.
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ hūṃ śiṣāye haḥ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ haṃ for the armor; ha hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ haḥ hūṃ phaṭ haḥ! To the weapon: haḥ hūṃ phaṭ!
Thus ends the Illumination of Mantras.
For each [deity], five oblations or three oblations should be offered.
Then one should perform the expulsion from the country and the expulsion at the [appropriate] time.
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, for the eradication of the region, svāhā!
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, svāhā to the one who causes the destruction of time!
Having performed the pacification of the nine planets for the purpose of dispelling ill omens.
Then, with the root mantra, there is an offering of the prescribed number of oblations; [followed by] an oblation of rice and the worship of the Brahmins.
The offering of the *bali*: the inner *bali* and the outer *bali*. Having prepared two mandalas—the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the [outer] mandala—in the western mandala...
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Rudras! [In the] east.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Mothers! [In the south.]
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Gaṇas. In the west.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the yakṣas! [In the north.]
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the planets! To Īśa!
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Asuras! [In the southeast.]
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the rākṣasas! [In the] south-west.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Nāgas! [In the northwest.]
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the constellations! [Offer this] in the northeast, in the center of the maṇḍala.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the zodiac signs! [Offer this] into the fire.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to all the Viśvedevas! In the southwest.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Kṣetrapāla in the middle between Varuṇa and Anila.
Thus ends the procedure for the internal oblation.
Then, in the second mandala in the southeast.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Indra! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Agni!
Oṃ hāṃ yamāya svāhā || Oṃ hāṃ naiṛtyāya svāhā ||
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Varuṇa! Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Vāyu!
Oṃ hāṃ to Kubera, svāhā! Oṃ to Īśāna, svāhā!
From the east to the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā.
Aiming toward the upper portion in the northeast: Oṃ hāṃ Viṣṇave svāhā.
Aiming toward the lower part, in the direction of the southwest.
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Kṣetrapāla. Between those two:
Then, outside the mandala, one offers the outer bali with the mantra "svāhā to the crows and others who violate the samaya. Having thus given the bali:
One should dissolve [the deity] into oneself by means of the withdrawal mudrā. [This is] the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa). Having performed the oblation of the Vārtika [verses],...
Having placed the *śruva* ladle with its opening facing downward over the *puṣkara*, and holding it crosswise at the navel with both the left and right hands,
one offers the full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, may there be water for sipping, svāhā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva, [this] fragrance.
One should offer four oblations with the *pūrṇāhuti* at the end.
Oṃ hāṃ bhūḥ svāhā || Oṃ hāṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā ||
Oṃ hāṃ svaḥ svāhā. Oṃ hāṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā. Thus.
Then, at the time of twilight, one should cause three mandalas to be prepared.

In the first, one should cause the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) to be offered with the heart-mantra; in the second, the sacrificial porridge (caru), in eight mouthfuls, without touching it with the teeth. In the third mandala, the tooth-stick (dantadhāvana) is offered.
One should observe its fall: [a fall] in the east, west, north, or northeast is auspicious.

In other cases of [unfavorable] falls, it is inauspicious. One should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) by offering oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra or another weapon mantra. Then one should cause [the deity] to sleep. Having spread *darbha* grass and a black antelope skin, one should [anoint the image] with ashes, mustard seeds, and the weapon mantra.
Having performed the protection ritual, one should recite the Svapnamānavaka mantra.
"Oṃ hili 2 śūlapāṇaye svāhā. Thus one should speak it into the right ear of the disciple.
At night, having offered a bali-oblation with the Aghora-weapon mantra, he himself should also take to bed.
[Thus ends the ritual procedure for the consecration.]
Again, at dawn, having performed the morning bath, one should report the dream to the guru.
One should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*) with the *Aghora* weapon-mantra or the [other] weapon-mantra over an impure substance; having offered the oblation (*āhuti*).
Then, having offered oblations to the deities of the directions, the doors, the water-pot, the sacrificial mound, and so forth;
For the purpose of initiating the disciple, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra; then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),

one should offer a hundred, a hundred, or two by two, together with the full oblation, with the root mantra for the sake of averting regional calamities, temporal calamities, the proclamation of ill omens, and for establishing auspicious omens.
Then, the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) with the mantra beginning "Oṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Śiva," and so forth;
and the illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantra beginning "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, hūṃ phaṭ to Śiva," and so forth, three times each.
The inner offering.
Then, having prepared the outer mandala outside the pavilion and holding kuśa grass with its tips pointing eastward,
one should designate a seat for the syllable *praṇava* and position the disciple facing east with his upper body upright.
Standing himself facing north, having applied the root mantra to his eyes, and having gazed at the disciple from the head down to the feet.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ! With the weapon-mantra ending in phaṭ, sprinkle the disciple with the water of the heavenly offering (arghya).

Having struck [the disciple] with ashes using this mantra, one should strike the tips and roots of the *kuśa* grass three times at the navel, both above and below, using this very same mantra. One should sprinkle [water] over the disciple with the *kavaca* mantra. Having visualized oneself as standing in the center of the four mandalas, one should strike one's own heart with the *astra* mantra and contemplate it in the form of a shimmering star.

Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Consciousness (Cetanyāya). Having restrained consciousness within the heart by means of the Niṣṭhurā [mudrā], and having worshipped its residence in the head and the heart with the eightfold offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā), one should cover the eyes with a clean cloth that has been consecrated with the Heart-mantra or the Eye-mantra, following the purification rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa). Holding a flower in the hand—
Having given [the offerings],
and having entered the sacrificial pavilion by way of circumambulation,
one should sit upon a seat prepared with six elevations on a mandala to the right of the deity.

Having purified the body of the disciple through the sequence of elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi) and performed the internal sacrifice and other rites, he should place that radiant Hand of Śiva upon the disciple's head.
Having contemplated that the disciple's body, both internally and externally, is pervaded by that splendor,

having offered a flower to Śiva, having opened [the disciple's] eyes, and having caused him to perform prostration to Śiva and the Self (Ātman), he should lead him to the vicinity of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and place him on his own right side upon a seat consisting of sixfold arising (ṣaḍutthāsana).

Having seated the disciple within the mandala, and having placed kusha grass with both root and tip upon his own shanks— the root on the disciple's hand and the tip on his own— he should worship Shiva residing in the fire with the eightfold offering of flowers (ashṭapuṣpikā).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Iḍā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Suṣumnā.
Having thus worshipped and offered five oblations for each with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*,
and having performed the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), one should pour [the remains] upon the head of the disciple;
then, for the sake of stabilizing the "Hand of Śiva" (*śivahasta*), one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra.
Having offered oblations with a tenth part of the [remaining] grains, having given the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*,

and having placed a drop of the *arghya* water on the head, one should cause the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) to be given. [Having offered one hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) for the sake of atonement.]
And having offered the full oblation, ||
[This is] the initiation according to the common convention.
